items.title: An Artinian integral domain is a field
items.strategy: Let $D$ be an Artinian integral domain and take $0 \ne a \in D$. The descending chain $(a) \supseteq (a^2) \supseteq \cdots$ stabilizes, so $(a^n)=(a^{n+1})$ for some $n$. Then $a^n=a^{n+1}b$ for some $b$, and cancellation in the domain gives $1=ab$, so every nonzero element is a unit.

items.title: Every prime ideal of an Artinian ring is maximal
items.strategy: If $\mathfrak p$ is prime in an Artinian ring $R$, then ideals of $R/\mathfrak p$ correspond to ideals of $R$ containing $\mathfrak p$, so $R/\mathfrak p$ is Artinian. The quotient is also a domain because $\mathfrak p$ is prime, and the preceding lemma makes that Artinian domain a field. Therefore $R/\mathfrak p$ is a field and $\mathfrak p$ is maximal.

items.title: An Artinian ring has only finitely many maximal ideals
items.strategy: Among the finite intersections of maximal ideals choose one minimal by inclusion. If some other maximal ideal $\mathfrak m$ were missing, then for each listed maximal ideal choose an element in it but not in $\mathfrak m$; their product still avoids $\mathfrak m$ because $\mathfrak m$ is prime, but lies in the chosen minimal intersection, contradiction.

items.title: The nilradical of an Artinian ring is a nilpotent ideal
items.strategy:
Let $N=\operatorname{Nil}(R)$. If $N^n=N^{n+1}$ with $N^n 
e 0$, choose an ideal $\mathfrak a$ minimal among those with $\mathfrak aN^n 
e 0$, then choose $a \in \mathfrak a$ with $aN^n 
e 0$. Minimality forces $\mathfrak a=(a)$ and $aN^n=(a)$, so $a=ax$ for some $x \in N^n$; iterating and using nilpotence of $x$ gives $a=0$, contradiction.

items.title: Chinese remainder theorem for pairwise comaximal ideals
items.strategy: For two comaximal ideals $I,J$, prove $IJ=I \cap J$, identify the kernel of $R \to R/I \times R/J$, and solve simultaneous residues using $u+v=1$ with $u \in I$, $v \in J$. Then show one ideal is comaximal with the product of the rest, so induction on the finite family yields the isomorphism $R/\prod I_i \cong \prod R/I_i$ together with $\bigcap I_i=\prod I_i$.

items.title: Every commutative Artinian ring is Noetherian
items.strategy: Let $N$ be the nilradical. By the preceding results, the maximal ideals are finite in number, $N$ is nilpotent, and $N=\bigcap \mathfrak m_i$; Chinese remainder identifies $R/N$ with a finite product of fields. For each layer $N^i/N^{i+1}$, use the orthogonal idempotents of $R/N$ to split it into field-vector-space components and prove inline that each component is finite-dimensional, since an infinite-dimensional component would yield a strict descending chain of subspaces and hence of ideals. Therefore every layer is Noetherian, and the finite $N$-adic filtration upgrades $R$ itself to Noetherian.

items.title: A commutative ring is Artinian exactly when it has finite length as a module over itself
items.strategy: If $R$ has finite length as an $R$-module, then its ideals satisfy both chain conditions, so $R$ is Artinian. Conversely, if $R$ is Artinian, the previous theorem makes its regular module both Artinian and Noetherian; the published module criterion then yields a composition series, hence finite length.

items.title: An Artinian local ring has nilpotent maximal ideal, and its finite modules have finite length
items.strategy: In a local Artinian ring the unique maximal ideal is the only prime ideal, hence the nilradical, so it is nilpotent. For a finite module $M$, the filtration $M \supseteq \mathfrak mM \supseteq \cdots \supseteq 0$ terminates; each quotient is killed by $\mathfrak m$ and is therefore a vector space over the residue field, and the images of one fixed finite generating set of $M$ generate every quotient, so each quotient is finite-dimensional. Additivity of length along the filtration yields finite length.

items.title: An Artinian ring is canonically the finite product of its localizations at its maximal ideals
items.strategy: Let $\mathfrak m_1,\dots,\mathfrak m_r$ be the maximal ideals and choose $n$ with $N^n=0$ for the nilradical $N$. The powers $\mathfrak m_i^n$ are pairwise comaximal and have zero product, so Chinese remainder gives $R \cong \prod_i R/\mathfrak m_i^n$. Each quotient is local with maximal ideal $\mathfrak m_i/\mathfrak m_i^n$, and comparison with localization at $\mathfrak m_i$ identifies these factors with the canonical local rings $R_{\mathfrak m_i}$; the quotient-by-powers presentation depends on the chosen exponent and is not called canonical.

items.title: The prime ideals of an Artinian ring are exactly its finitely many maximal ideals
items.strategy: Combine the theorem that every prime ideal is maximal with the theorem that only finitely many maximal ideals exist. Record just the finite-set identification here; the discrete-topology consequence waits for the later spectrum topology page.

items.title: A Noetherian ring is Artinian exactly when every prime ideal is maximal
items.strategy: The forward direction is the Artinian prime-maximal theorem together with Artinian implies Noetherian. Conversely, if $R$ is Noetherian and every prime is maximal, then the finitely many minimal primes over $(0)$ are all maximal and every prime contains one of them, hence equals one of them. The nilradical is nilpotent, the reduced quotient is a finite product of fields by Chinese remainder, and the nilpotent-radical filtration gives finite length for the regular module; therefore $R$ is Artinian.

items.title: Quotients and localizations of an Artinian ring are Artinian
items.strategy: A quotient of an Artinian ring is Artinian because its ideals correspond to ideals above the kernel. For localizations, use the Artinian product decomposition: localizing a finite product acts factorwise, and in a local Artinian factor a denominator in the maximal ideal kills the localization because that ideal is nilpotent, while a denominator outside the maximal ideal is already a unit. Thus a localization keeps exactly the local factors whose maximal ideals avoid the multiplicative set.

items.title: The truncated polynomial ring $k[x]/(x^n)$ is local Artinian of length $n$
items.strategy: Let $R=k[x]/(x^n)$ and $\mathfrak m=(x)$. Show $\mathfrak m^n=0$, every ideal is $(x^r)$ for some $0 \le r \le n$, and each quotient $\mathfrak m^r/\mathfrak m^{r+1}$ is one-dimensional over $k=R/\mathfrak m$. The filtration by powers of $\mathfrak m$ then gives the ring length and makes the nilpotent maximal ideal explicit.

items.title: $\mathbb Z/12\mathbb Z$ splits as the product of its two local Artinian factors
items.strategy: Use the Chinese remainder theorem to identify $\mathbb Z/12\mathbb Z$ with $\mathbb Z/3\mathbb Z \times \mathbb Z/4\mathbb Z$. Check that the two factors are local, read off the two prime ideals of the product, and pull them back to the two primes of $\mathbb Z/12\mathbb Z$ to see the structure theorem concretely.

items.title: A field has module length one over itself
items.strategy: For a field $K$, the chain $0 \subset K$ is a composition series, so $\ell_K(K)=1$. Hence every field is Artinian and gives the minimal nonzero example for the page's length convention.

items.title: $\mathbb Z$ and $k[x]$ are Noetherian but not Artinian
items.strategy: Use the published Noetherian results for $\mathbb Z$ and for finite-variable polynomial rings. Then exhibit the strict descending ideal chains $(2) \supset (2^2) \supset \cdots$ in $\mathbb Z$ and $(x) \supset (x^2) \supset \cdots$ in $k[x]$ to show that Noetherianity alone does not force Artinianness.

items.title: The module $R/(x^i)$ over $k[x]/(x^n)$ has length $i$
items.strategy: Let $R=k[x]/(x^n)$ and $1 \le i \le n$. Filter $R/(x^i)$ by the images of $(x^j)$, so each subquotient is generated by one class killed by $(x)$ and hence is one-dimensional over the residue field. The short exact sequences $0 \to (x^{i-1})/(x^i) \to R/(x^i) \to R/(x^{i-1}) \to 0$ then verify additivity step by step.

items.title: The ring $(\mathbb Z/2)^{\mathbb N}$ is zero-dimensional but not Noetherian
items.strategy: In $R=(\mathbb Z/2)^{\mathbb N}$ every element is idempotent coordinatewise. Therefore if $\mathfrak p$ is prime then every element of the domain $R/\mathfrak p$ satisfies $x^2=x$, so every nonzero class equals $1$ and the quotient is a field; thus every prime is maximal. On the other hand the ideals generated by the first finitely many coordinate idempotents form a strict ascending chain, so $R$ is not Noetherian and hence not Artinian.
